questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: How many atoms in all are present in 4.4 g of carbon dioxide? (C = 12, O = 16, Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)

solution.concept: Mole concept: moles = mass / molar mass; atoms = moles of molecules × atoms per molecule × Nₐ
solution.explanation: Find the moles of CO₂ first. Each CO₂ molecule has three atoms (one C and two O).
steps: Molar mass of CO₂ = 12 + 2 × 16 = 44 g mol⁻¹
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.022 × 10²² counts molecules, not atoms. 1.204 × 10²³ counts only the oxygen atoms. 1.807 × 10²⁴ treats the 4.4 g sample as one mole of CO₂.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (law) with List-II (scientist who proposed it).

List-I:
A. Law of conservation of mass
B. Law of definite proportions
C. Law of gaseous volumes
D. Law of multiple proportions

List-II:
I. Joseph Proust
II. Antoine Lavoisier
III. Joseph Gay-Lussac
IV. John Dalton

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Laws of chemical combination and the scientists who stated them
solution.explanation: Lavoisier stated that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. Proust found that a given compound always contains the same elements in the same proportion by mass. Gay-Lussac observed that gases combine in simple whole-number ratios by volume. Dalton proposed the law of multiple proportions.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry', laws of chemical combinations
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The percentage by mass of nitrogen in urea, CO(NH₂)₂, is (C = 12, N = 14, O = 16, H = 1):

solution.concept: Mass per cent of an element in a compound
solution.explanation: Mass per cent = (mass of the element in one mole of the compound / molar mass) × 100. Urea has two nitrogen atoms per molecule.
steps: Molar mass of urea = 12 + 16 + 2 × (14 + 2) = 60 g mol⁻¹
Mass of N per mole = 2 × 14 = 28 g
solution.why_others_wrong: 23.3% counts only one nitrogen atom. 26.7% is the mass per cent of oxygen and 20.0% that of carbon.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 4 g of hydrogen gas is mixed with 40 g of oxygen gas and the mixture is exploded. The maximum mass of water that can be formed is (H = 1, O = 16):

solution.concept: Limiting reagent
solution.explanation: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Find which reactant runs out first; it alone decides how much product forms.
steps: Moles of H₂ = 4/2 = 2 mol; moles of O₂ = 40/32 = 1.25 mol
2 mol H₂ needs only 1 mol O₂, and 1.25 mol is available → H₂ is the limiting reagent
2 mol H₂ gives 2 mol H₂O = 2 × 18 = 36 g (0.25 mol O₂ is left over)
solution.why_others_wrong: 45 g takes O₂ as the limiting reagent (1.25 mol O₂ would need 2.5 mol H₂). 44 g simply adds the masses and ignores the unused oxygen. 18 g wrongly takes 2 mol H₂ to give 1 mol water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen by mass. Its molar mass is 56 g mol⁻¹. Its molecular formula is (C = 12, H = 1):

solution.concept: Empirical formula from mass per cent, then molecular formula from molar mass
solution.explanation: Divide each mass per cent by the atomic mass to get relative moles, reduce to the simplest whole-number ratio, then multiply the empirical formula by n = molar mass / empirical formula mass.
steps: Ratio C : H = 7.14 : 14.3 = 1 : 2 → empirical formula CH₂ (mass 14)
solution.why_others_wrong: CH₂ is only the empirical formula. C₂H₄ has the right ratio but a molar mass of 28. C₄H₁₀ has mass 58 and a C : H ratio of 2 : 5.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): 1 g of O₂ and 1 g of O₃ contain the same number of oxygen atoms.
Reason (R): O₂ and O₃ have the same molar mass.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Moles of atoms in equal masses of allotropes
solution.explanation: Both samples are made only of oxygen atoms, so equal masses contain equal numbers of oxygen atoms: 1 g contains 1/16 mol of O atoms either way. A is true. The molar masses are different (32 and 48 g mol⁻¹), so R is false.
steps: O₂: 1/32 mol molecules × 2 = 1/16 mol O atoms
O₃: 1/48 mol molecules × 3 = 1/16 mol O atoms → A true
Molar mass of O₂ = 32 g mol⁻¹, of O₃ = 48 g mol⁻¹ → R false
solution.why_others_wrong: The numbers of molecules differ (O₂ has more molecules); only the numbers of atoms are equal.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: One mole of water contains 6.022 × 10²³ atoms.
Statement II: The mass of one mole of electrons is about 0.55 mg (mass of an electron = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹).

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Counting particles in a mole
solution.explanation: One mole of water contains 6.022 × 10²³ molecules. Each molecule has three atoms, so it contains 3 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.807 × 10²⁴ atoms: Statement I is false. One mole of electrons has a mass of 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 6.022 × 10²³ = 5.49 × 10⁻⁷ kg = 0.55 mg: Statement II is true.
steps: 1 mol H₂O = Nₐ molecules = 3Nₐ atoms → Statement I false
Mass of 1 mol e⁻ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg × 6.022 × 10²³ = 5.49 × 10⁻⁷ kg ≈ 0.55 mg → Statement II true
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 25 g of a limestone sample containing 80% CaCO₃ by mass (the rest being inert, non-volatile impurities) is heated strongly until no more CO₂ is given off: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. The mass of CaO formed is (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16):

solution.concept: Stoichiometry with an impure reactant
solution.explanation: Only the CaCO₃ in the sample decomposes. Find its moles, then use the 1 : 1 mole ratio with CaO.
steps: Mass of CaCO₃ = 80% of 25 g = 20 g
Moles of CaO = 0.2 mol → mass = 0.2 × 56 = 11.2 g
solution.why_others_wrong: 14.0 g ignores the impurity and treats all 25 g as CaCO₃. 8.8 g is the mass of CO₂ given off. 16.2 g is the mass of the whole residue (CaO plus 5 g of impurity), not of CaO alone.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Complete combustion of 0.1 mol of a hydrocarbon gives 13.2 g of CO₂ and 5.4 g of H₂O. The molecular formula of the hydrocarbon is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16):

solution.concept: Molecular formula from combustion data
solution.explanation: All the carbon of the hydrocarbon ends up in CO₂ and all its hydrogen in H₂O. Each H₂O carries two H atoms.
steps: Moles of CO₂ = 13.2/44 = 0.3 mol → 0.3 mol C from 0.1 mol compound → 3 C per molecule
Moles of H₂O = 5.4/18 = 0.3 mol → 0.6 mol H → 6 H per molecule
solution.why_others_wrong: C₃H₃ forgets that each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms. C₃H₈ assumes the compound is an alkane instead of using the data. CH₂ is only the empirical formula; the moles of compound fix the molecular formula.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following samples contain exactly one mole of atoms (6.022 × 10²³ atoms)? (H = 1, He = 4, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16)

(a) 12 g of carbon-12
(b) 9 g of water
(c) 4 g of helium
(d) 8 g of oxygen gas (O₂)
(e) 14 g of nitrogen gas (N₂)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Moles of atoms = moles of molecules × atoms per molecule
solution.explanation: Convert each mass to moles of the species, then multiply by the number of atoms in each species.
solution.why_others_wrong: Nitrogen gas is diatomic, so 14 g (half a mole of N₂) still gives one mole of atoms; water has three atoms per molecule, so 9 g gives 1.5 mol of atoms.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following sets of quantum numbers (n, l, mₗ, mₛ) is NOT possible for an electron in an atom?

solution.concept: Allowed values of quantum numbers
solution.explanation: l can take values 0 to (n − 1), mₗ from −l to +l, and mₛ is +½ or −½. For n = 2, l can only be 0 or 1.
steps: n = 2, l = 2: l must be less than n → not allowed
n = 2, l = 1, mₗ = 0: a 2p electron → allowed
n = 3, l = 2, mₗ = −2: a 3d electron → allowed
n = 4, l = 0, mₗ = 0: a 4s electron → allowed
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', quantum numbers
solution.final_answer: Option C: n = 2, l = 2, mₗ = +1, mₛ = +½

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The ground-state electronic configuration of the Fe²⁺ ion (Z of Fe = 26) is:

solution.concept: Electronic configuration of transition-metal cations
solution.explanation: Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². When a transition metal forms a cation, the 4s electrons are removed before the 3d electrons.
solution.why_others_wrong: [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s² removes the electrons from 3d instead of 4s. [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² is neutral Fe. [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ has the right count but a wrong distribution for the ion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Using Bohr's model, the radius of the second orbit (n = 2) of the He⁺ ion is (radius of the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen = 52.9 pm):

solution.concept: Radius of a Bohr orbit for a hydrogen-like species: rₙ = 52.9 n²/Z pm
solution.explanation: The radius grows as n² and shrinks as the nuclear charge Z grows. He⁺ has Z = 2 and one electron.
solution.why_others_wrong: 52.9 pm uses n instead of n². 211.6 pm ignores Z. 423.2 pm multiplies by Z instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', Bohr's model for hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The de Broglie wavelength of a moving particle is inversely proportional to its momentum.
Statement II: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle has a significant effect on the motion of macroscopic objects such as a cricket ball.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: de Broglie relation and the uncertainty principle
solution.explanation: λ = h/p = h/mv, so the wavelength is inversely proportional to momentum: Statement I is true. Because h is so small, the uncertainties for objects of ordinary mass are negligible; the principle matters only for microscopic particles such as electrons: Statement II is false.
steps: λ = h/mv → λ ∝ 1/p → Statement I true
Δx·Δv ≥ h/4πm: for m of about 0.1 kg the product is negligible → Statement II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', dual behaviour of matter and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The ratio of the wavelength of the first line of the Balmer series to that of the first line of the Lyman series in the hydrogen spectrum is:

solution.concept: Rydberg formula: 1/λ = R_H (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²)
solution.explanation: The first line of a series is the transition from the next higher level: 3 → 2 for Balmer, 2 → 1 for Lyman. Wavelength is inversely proportional to (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²).
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 : 27 is the ratio of the wave numbers (or frequencies), the inverse of what is asked. 9 : 4 and 4 : 1 compare squares of single quantum numbers instead of energy differences.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', line spectrum of hydrogen

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Particle P has four times the mass of particle Q. Their de Broglie wavelengths are in the ratio λ_P : λ_Q = 1 : 2. The ratio of their speeds v_P : v_Q is:

solution.concept: de Broglie relation λ = h/mv
solution.explanation: Rearranged, v = h/(mλ), so speed is inversely proportional to the product of mass and wavelength.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 : 1 inverts the answer. 1 : 8 and 8 : 1 multiply the mass ratio by the wavelength ratio instead of letting them act in opposite directions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (orbital) with List-II (numbers of radial and angular nodes).

List-I:
A. 2s
B. 3p
C. 3d
D. 4s

List-II:
I. 0 radial, 2 angular
II. 3 radial, 0 angular
III. 1 radial, 0 angular
IV. 1 radial, 1 angular

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Nodes of an orbital
solution.explanation: An orbital has (n − l − 1) radial nodes and l angular nodes, so (n − 1) nodes in all.
steps: 2s: n − l − 1 = 1 radial, l = 0 angular → III
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', shapes of atomic orbitals
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers.
(b) Pairing of electrons in orbitals of equal energy (such as the three p orbitals) does not take place until each of them has one electron.
(c) The total number of orbitals in a shell with principal quantum number n is n².
(d) A single 2p orbital can hold up to six electrons.
(e) The (n + l) value of a 4s orbital is greater than that of a 3d orbital.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Pauli exclusion principle, Hund's rule and orbital counting
solution.explanation: (a) is the Pauli exclusion principle and (b) is Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity. A shell n has n² orbitals. Any one orbital holds at most two electrons; six is the capacity of the whole 2p subshell. For 4s, n + l = 4 + 0 = 4; for 3d it is 3 + 2 = 5, which is why 4s fills first.
steps: (d) False: one orbital holds at most 2 electrons
(e) False: 4s has n + l = 4, 3d has n + l = 5
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', filling of orbitals in atoms

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The ground-state electronic configuration of copper (Z = 29) is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ and not [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s².
Reason (R): Completely filled and exactly half-filled subshells have extra stability because of their symmetrical distribution and larger exchange energy.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Stability of completely filled and half-filled subshells
solution.explanation: Moving one electron from 4s to 3d gives copper a completely filled 3d¹⁰ subshell. Such subshells (and half-filled ones) are extra stable because of symmetry and larger exchange energy. R is true and is exactly why A is true.
steps: Reason: symmetry and exchange energy stabilise d¹⁰ → R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', stability of completely filled and half-filled subshells
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The uncertainty in the position of an electron is 0.1 nm. The minimum uncertainty in its velocity is (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mass of electron = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg):

solution.concept: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: Δx · m Δv ≥ h/4π
solution.explanation: Convert Δx to metres and rearrange for the smallest Δv.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.27 × 10⁶ leaves out 4π. 1.16 × 10⁶ uses h/2π instead of h/4π. 5.79 × 10⁴ takes Δx as 1 nm.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', Heisenberg's uncertainty principle

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In a sample of hydrogen atoms, electrons are excited to the n = 5 level. When they return to the ground state by all possible routes, how many different spectral lines can appear in all, and how many of them belong to the Balmer series?

options.text: 10 lines in all, 4 of them in the Balmer series
10 lines in all, 3 of them in the Balmer series
4 lines in all, 1 of them in the Balmer series
15 lines in all, 3 of them in the Balmer series

solution.concept: Number of spectral lines from level n: n(n − 1)/2
solution.explanation: Every pair of levels from 1 to 5 gives one line. The Balmer series contains only the transitions that end on n = 2.
steps: Balmer lines end on n = 2: 5 → 2, 4 → 2, 3 → 2 → 3 lines
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 Balmer lines wrongly counts 2 → 1 (a Lyman line) or a 6 → 2 line that cannot occur here. 4 lines in all is the most one single atom can emit (n − 1), not a whole sample. 15 uses n(n + 1)/2.
solution.final_answer: Option B: 10 lines in all, 3 of them in the Balmer series

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The ionisation energy of a hydrogen atom in its ground state is 13.6 eV. The energy needed to remove the electron from the n = 2 level of the Li²⁺ ion (Z = 3) is:

solution.concept: Energy of a level in a hydrogen-like species: Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV
solution.explanation: Removing the electron from level n needs energy equal to |Eₙ|.
solution.why_others_wrong: 122.4 eV is the ionisation energy from n = 1. 10.2 eV uses Z instead of Z². 61.2 eV uses n instead of n².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', Bohr's model for hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a hydrogen atom, the 2s orbital is lower in energy than the 2p orbital.
Reason (R): In atoms with more than one electron, the energy of an orbital depends on both n and l.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Energies of orbitals in hydrogen and in multi-electron atoms
solution.explanation: In the hydrogen atom, the energy of an orbital depends only on n, so 2s and 2p are degenerate: A is false. In multi-electron atoms, electron–electron repulsion and shielding make the energy depend on both n and l (2s < 2p): R is true.
steps: Hydrogen: energy depends on n only → 2s = 2p → A false
Multi-electron atoms: energy depends on n and l → R true
solution.why_others_wrong: The trap is to apply the multi-electron order (2s < 2p) to hydrogen.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', energies of orbitals
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The shape of the ClF₃ molecule is:

solution.concept: VSEPR theory: 3 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs
solution.explanation: Cl has 7 valence electrons; 3 form bonds with F and 4 remain as 2 lone pairs. Five electron pairs take a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement with both lone pairs equatorial, leaving a T shape.
steps: Cl: 7 valence electrons → 3 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs = 5 pairs
Lone pairs occupy equatorial positions to reduce lone pair–lone pair repulsion
The three F atoms and Cl form a T shape
solution.why_others_wrong: Trigonal planar needs 3 bond pairs and no lone pair (BF₃). Trigonal pyramidal needs 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair (NH₃). See-saw needs 4 bond pairs and 1 lone pair (SF₄).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', VSEPR theory

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In which of the following molecules is the central atom sp hybridised?

solution.concept: Hybridisation from the number of electron pairs around the central atom
solution.explanation: Be in BeCl₂ forms two bonds and has no lone pair, so one 2s and one 2p orbital mix to give two sp hybrid orbitals at 180°: the molecule is linear.
steps: BeCl₂: 2 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → sp, linear
H₂O: 2 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs → sp³
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', hybridisation

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The O₂ molecule is paramagnetic.
Reason (R): The O₂ molecule contains an even number of electrons.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Magnetic behaviour from molecular orbital theory
solution.explanation: O₂ has 16 electrons, an even number, so R is true. But an even total does not decide magnetism: in O₂ the last two electrons go singly into the two degenerate π*2p orbitals (Hund's rule), giving two unpaired electrons, so O₂ is paramagnetic. A is true, but R does not explain it.
steps: O₂: KK σ2s² σ*2s² σ2p_z² π2p_x² π2p_y² π*2p_x¹ π*2p_y¹
Two unpaired electrons → paramagnetic → A true
16 electrons is even → R true, but it is the unpaired π* electrons that cause paramagnetism
solution.why_others_wrong: Option A is the trap: an even electron count would, if anything, suggest diamagnetism.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', bonding in some homonuclear diatomic molecules
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Formation of an ionic bond is favoured by a high ionisation enthalpy of the metal atom.
Statement II: Lattice enthalpy of an ionic solid is the energy required to completely separate one mole of the solid into its gaseous ions.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Factors favouring ionic bonding; lattice enthalpy
solution.explanation: An ionic bond forms more easily when the metal loses electrons easily (low ionisation enthalpy) and the non-metal gains them readily: Statement I is false. Statement II is the definition of lattice enthalpy.
steps: Low ionisation enthalpy of the metal favours cation formation → Statement I false
Lattice enthalpy: solid → gaseous ions, per mole → Statement II true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', ionic or electrovalent bond and lattice enthalpy
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following molecules has zero dipole moment?

solution.concept: Dipole moment depends on bond polarity and molecular geometry
solution.explanation: BF₃ is trigonal planar and symmetrical; the three B–F bond dipoles are at 120° and cancel.
steps: BF₃: trigonal planar, bond dipoles cancel → μ = 0
NH₃ and NF₃: pyramidal → net dipole
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', polarity of bonds

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (species) with List-II (bond order from molecular orbital theory).

List-I:
A. N₂
B. O₂
C. O₂⁺
D. O₂²⁻

List-II:
I. 1
II. 2
III. 2.5
IV. 3

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Bond order = ½ (Nb − Na)
solution.explanation: Fill the molecular orbitals with all the electrons of the species and count bonding (Nb) and antibonding (Na) electrons. Valence-shell counting gives the same result.
solution.shortcut: Removing an electron from O₂ (from π*) raises the bond order by ½; adding one lowers it by ½.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', bond order
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The H–N–H bond angle in NH₃ (about 107°) is smaller than the H–C–H bond angle in CH₄ (109.5°).
Reason (R): Lone pair–bond pair repulsion is stronger than bond pair–bond pair repulsion.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: VSEPR: order of electron-pair repulsions
solution.explanation: Both molecules have four electron pairs around the central atom. In NH₃ one of them is a lone pair, which repels the bond pairs more strongly than they repel each other, squeezing the H–N–H angle below the tetrahedral value. R is true and explains A.
steps: lp–bp > bp–bp repulsion → angle reduced to about 107°
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', VSEPR theory
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
In which of the following species is the central atom sp³d² hybridised?

(a) SF₆
(b) PCl₅
(c) IF₅
(d) SF₄
(e) [SiF₆]²⁻

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Hybridisation from the number of electron pairs (bond pairs + lone pairs)
solution.explanation: Six electron pairs around the central atom need six hybrid orbitals: sp³d². Five pairs need sp³d.
steps: (c) IF₅: 5 bond pairs + 1 lone pair → sp³d² (square pyramidal)
(d) SF₄: 4 bond pairs + 1 lone pair → sp³d
solution.why_others_wrong: IF₅ is easy to miss: its lone pair counts as the sixth electron pair.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: NF₃ has a much smaller dipole moment than NH₃, although both molecules are pyramidal.
Statement II: In NH₃ the orbital dipole of the lone pair is in the same direction as the resultant of the N–H bond dipoles, whereas in NF₃ it is opposite to the resultant of the N–F bond dipoles.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Dipole moment as a vector sum including the lone pair
solution.explanation: In NH₃, N is more electronegative than H, so the bond dipoles point towards N, the same way as the lone pair: they add. In NF₃, F is more electronegative than N, so the bond dipoles point away from N, opposing the lone pair: they partly cancel. Both statements are true (and II explains I).
steps: NH₃: bond dipoles towards N + lone pair → add → larger μ (about 1.47 D)
NF₃: bond dipoles towards F oppose the lone pair → smaller μ (about 0.23 D)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', polarity of bonds
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): o-Nitrophenol is steam volatile, whereas p-nitrophenol is not.
Reason (R): o-Nitrophenol has intramolecular hydrogen bonding, whereas p-nitrophenol molecules are associated through intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Intramolecular versus intermolecular hydrogen bonding
solution.explanation: In o-nitrophenol the –OH and –NO₂ groups are next to each other and form a hydrogen bond within the same molecule, so the molecules do not associate and the compound is volatile. In p-nitrophenol the groups are far apart, so hydrogen bonds form between molecules; the association lowers volatility. R explains A.
steps: ortho: intramolecular H-bond → no association → steam volatile
para: intermolecular H-bonds → associated molecules → less volatile
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', physical properties of phenols
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The two O–O bonds in ozone have the same length (128 pm), which lies between the O–O single bond (148 pm) and the O=O double bond (121 pm) lengths.
Statement II: The ozone molecule keeps switching rapidly between its two canonical (resonance) structures.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Resonance: the resonance hybrid is the real structure
solution.explanation: Experiment shows both O–O bonds in O₃ are equal and intermediate between single and double bonds: Statement I is true. The canonical forms are only ways of writing the structure; they have no real existence and the molecule does not oscillate between them: Statement II is false.
steps: Equal O–O bonds of 128 pm → resonance hybrid → Statement I true
Canonical structures do not exist on their own; there is no switching → Statement II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', resonance structures
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In a Lewis structure of the nitrate ion (NO₃⁻) with one N=O double bond and two N–O single bonds, the formal charge on the nitrogen atom is:

solution.concept: Formal charge = valence electrons − non-bonding electrons − ½ (bonding electrons)
solution.explanation: Nitrogen forms four bonds in this structure (one double + two single) and has no lone pair.
solution.why_others_wrong: +5 is the oxidation number of nitrogen in nitrate, not its formal charge. −1 is the formal charge on each singly bonded oxygen (and the overall ion charge). 0 is the formal charge of the doubly bonded oxygen.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', formal charge

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): N₂⁺ and N₂⁻ have the same bond order.
Reason (R): N₂⁺ and N₂⁻ are both diamagnetic.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Bond order and magnetism of N₂ ions
solution.explanation: N₂⁺ (13 electrons) loses a bonding σ2p electron: bond order (9 − 4)/2 = 2.5. N₂⁻ (15 electrons) gains an antibonding π* electron: bond order (10 − 5)/2 = 2.5. A is true. Each ion has one unpaired electron, so both are paramagnetic: R is false.
steps: N₂⁺: Nb = 9, Na = 4 → 2.5, one unpaired electron
N₂⁻: Nb = 10, Na = 5 → 2.5, one unpaired electron
Same bond order → A true; both paramagnetic → R false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', molecular orbital theory
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
In which of the following pairs do both molecules have the same shape?

(a) XeF₂ and CO₂
(b) NH₃ and BF₃
(c) CH₄ and XeF₄
(d) H₂O and SO₂
(e) PCl₅ and BrF₅

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Shape depends on bond pairs and lone pairs together
solution.explanation: Count bond pairs and lone pairs on each central atom; lone pairs change the shape even when the number of electron pairs is the same.
steps: (a) XeF₂ (2 bp + 3 lp) linear; CO₂ linear → same
(b) NH₃ pyramidal; BF₃ trigonal planar → different
(c) CH₄ tetrahedral; XeF₄ (4 bp + 2 lp) square planar → different
(d) H₂O (2 bp + 2 lp) bent; SO₂ (2 σ bonds + 1 lp on S) bent → same
(e) PCl₅ trigonal bipyramidal; BrF₅ square pyramidal → different
solution.why_others_wrong: XeF₂ looks crowded, but its three lone pairs sit in the equatorial plane and leave the molecule linear.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', VSEPR theory

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (molecule) with List-II (shape).

List-I:
A. XeF₄
B. SF₄
C. BrF₅
D. ClF₃

List-II:
I. Square pyramidal
II. T-shaped
III. Square planar
IV. See-saw

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Shapes of molecules with lone pairs on the central atom (VSEPR)
solution.explanation: Count bond pairs and lone pairs on the central atom, place the electron pairs to minimise repulsion (lone pairs equatorial in a trigonal bipyramid, opposite each other in an octahedron) and name the shape from the positions of the atoms only.
steps: XeF₄: 4 bp + 2 lp (6 pairs, octahedral arrangement, lone pairs trans) → square planar → III
SF₄: 4 bp + 1 lp (5 pairs, lone pair equatorial) → see-saw → IV
BrF₅: 5 bp + 1 lp (6 pairs, octahedral arrangement) → square pyramidal → I
ClF₃: 3 bp + 2 lp (5 pairs, both lone pairs equatorial) → T-shaped → II
solution.why_others_wrong: Option A swaps XeF₄ and BrF₅, which both have six electron pairs. Option B swaps SF₄ and ClF₃, which both have five electron pairs. Option C gives BrF₅ the T shape and ClF₃ the square pyramid, mixing up a six-pair and a five-pair molecule.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', VSEPR theory
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The C₂ molecule is diamagnetic.
Statement II: The double bond in C₂ consists of one σ bond and one π bond.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Molecular orbital configuration of C₂
solution.explanation: C₂ has 12 electrons: KK σ2s² σ*2s² π2p_x² π2p_y². All electrons are paired, so C₂ is diamagnetic: Statement I is true. Its bond order is 2, but both bonds come from the two filled π orbitals; there is no electron in σ2p_z. So the double bond is made of two π bonds: Statement II is false.
steps: 12 electrons fill up to π2p_x² π2p_y² (σ2p_z is empty)
All paired → diamagnetic → Statement I true
Bond order 2 from four π electrons → two π bonds → Statement II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', bonding in some homonuclear diatomic molecules
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following orders of covalent character is correct?

solution.concept: Fajans' rules: covalent character of ionic bonds
solution.explanation: Covalent character increases as the cation becomes smaller and more highly charged (more polarising) and as the anion becomes larger (more polarisable).
steps: Li⁺ < Na⁺ < K⁺ in size → polarising power Li⁺ > Na⁺ > K⁺ → LiCl > NaCl > KCl (correct)
I⁻ is the largest anion → LiI is the most covalent of the lithium halides, so LiF > LiCl > LiI is reversed
Al³⁺ is smallest and most charged → AlCl₃ > MgCl₂ > NaCl, so that option is reversed
KCl > NaCl > LiCl is the reverse of the correct order
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', polarity of bonds (Fajans' rules)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (type of process) with List-II (quantity that stays zero or constant).

List-I:
A. Isothermal process
B. Adiabatic process
C. Isochoric process
D. Isobaric process

List-II:
I. q = 0
II. ΔT = 0
III. Δp = 0
IV. ΔV = 0

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Types of thermodynamic processes
solution.explanation: Each process is named after the quantity that does not change: iso-thermal (temperature), adiabatic (no heat exchange), iso-choric (volume), iso-baric (pressure).
steps: Adiabatic: no heat exchanged → q = 0 → I
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a state function?

solution.concept: State functions and path functions
solution.explanation: A state function depends only on the state of the system, not on how it got there. Work and heat depend on the path; U, H and S do not.
steps: U, H and S: fixed by the state → state functions
w: depends on the path (e.g. reversible or irreversible) → not a state function
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', state functions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For an isolated system, ΔU = 0.
Statement II: For a spontaneous process in an isolated system, the change in entropy is positive.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Isolated systems and the entropy criterion
solution.explanation: An isolated system exchanges neither energy nor matter with the surroundings, so its internal energy cannot change: Statement I is true. For such a system, a spontaneous process is one in which entropy increases (ΔS > 0): Statement II is true.
steps: Isolated: q = 0, w = 0 → ΔU = 0 → Statement I true
Spontaneous change in isolated system: ΔS > 0 → Statement II true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', first law and entropy
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For which of the following substances is the standard enthalpy of formation, ΔfH°, equal to zero at 298 K?

solution.concept: Standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its reference state is zero
solution.explanation: ΔfH° is zero only for an element in its most stable (reference) form at 1 bar and 298 K. Bromine's reference state at 298 K is the liquid.
steps: Br₂(l): reference state of bromine → ΔfH° = 0
O₃(g): not the reference form of oxygen (O₂ is) → ≠ 0
C(diamond): reference form of carbon is graphite → ≠ 0
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', standard enthalpy of formation

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For the reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92.4 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. Treating the gases as ideal, ΔU for the reaction at 298 K is (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹):

solution.concept: Relation between ΔH and ΔU: ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT
solution.explanation: Δn_g is the change in the number of moles of gas from reactants to products.
solution.why_others_wrong: −97.4 kJ adds Δn_g RT instead of subtracting it. −92.4 kJ assumes ΔU = ΔH. −89.9 kJ takes Δn_g = −1.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', relation between ΔH and ΔU

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Given: C(graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g); ΔH = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹ and CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g); ΔH = −283.0 kJ mol⁻¹. The standard enthalpy of formation of CO(g) is:

solution.concept: Hess's law of constant heat summation
solution.explanation: Formation of CO: C(graphite) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g). Get it by taking the first equation and reversing the second.
steps: Add: C + ½O₂ → CO; ΔH = −393.5 + 283.0 = −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹
solution.why_others_wrong: −676.5 adds the two equations without reversing the second. +110.5 has the sign wrong. −221.0 is the value for forming 2 mol of CO.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', Hess's law of constant heat summation

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Every exothermic reaction is spontaneous.
Reason (R): ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, so the sign of ΔG depends on both ΔH and TΔS.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Gibbs energy criterion for spontaneity
solution.explanation: A negative ΔH helps, but if ΔS is negative and T is high enough, −TΔS can outweigh ΔH and make ΔG positive. So exothermic reactions are not always spontaneous: A is false. R is the correct relation and is true.
steps: ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0 → ΔG > 0 at high T → not spontaneous
So A is false; R is true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', Gibbs energy and spontaneity
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A liquid boils at 350 K and its enthalpy of vaporisation is 31.5 kJ mol⁻¹. The entropy of vaporisation at its boiling point is:

solution.concept: Entropy change for a phase change at equilibrium: ΔS = ΔH/T
solution.explanation: At the boiling point, liquid and vapour are in equilibrium, so ΔvapS = ΔvapH / Tb. Convert kJ to J.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.09 forgets to convert kJ to J. 11.1 divides T by ΔH. −90 has the wrong sign: vaporisation increases disorder.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (enthalpy change) with List-II (process it refers to).

List-I:
A. Standard enthalpy of formation of methane
B. Enthalpy of combustion of methane
C. Enthalpy of atomisation of methane
D. Enthalpy of fusion of ice

List-II:
I. CH₄(g) → C(g) + 4H(g)
II. CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)
III. H₂O(s) → H₂O(l)
IV. C(graphite) + 2H₂(g) → CH₄(g)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Types of enthalpy changes
solution.explanation: Formation starts from elements in their reference states; combustion burns one mole completely in oxygen; atomisation breaks all bonds to give gaseous atoms; fusion melts the solid.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', enthalpies for different types of reactions
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The standard Gibbs energy change of a reaction at 298 K is −11.42 kJ mol⁻¹. Its equilibrium constant at this temperature is (2.303 RT = 5.71 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K):

solution.concept: ΔG° = −2.303 RT log K
solution.explanation: Rearrange for log K and take the antilog.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.01 drops the minus sign (log K = −2). 7.39 uses e² by treating 5.71 kJ as RT. 2 is log K, not K.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', Gibbs energy change and equilibrium

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For a decomposition reaction, ΔH = +176 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +160 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Assuming both stay constant with temperature, the reaction becomes spontaneous above:

solution.concept: Temperature at which ΔG changes sign: T = ΔH/ΔS
solution.explanation: With ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS becomes negative once TΔS exceeds ΔH.
steps: T = 176 000 J mol⁻¹ / 160 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 1100 K
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.1 K leaves ΔH in kJ. 827 K is the Celsius value (1100 − 273) written as kelvin. 1373 K adds 273 to a value that is already in kelvin.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) For the free expansion of an ideal gas into vacuum, w = 0.
(b) For the isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, ΔU = 0.
(c) For the reversible isothermal expansion of n mol of an ideal gas from Vᵢ to V_f, w = −2.303 nRT log (V_f/Vᵢ).
(d) The enthalpy change of a reaction equals the heat absorbed at constant volume.
(e) For one mole of an ideal gas, C_p − C_v = R.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: First law applied to ideal gases
solution.explanation: Free expansion is against zero external pressure, so no work is done. The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature. Heat at constant volume equals ΔU, while heat at constant pressure equals ΔH.
steps: (b) True: U of an ideal gas depends only on T
(d) False: q_v = ΔU; it is q_p that equals ΔH
(e) True: C_p − C_v = R for one mole of ideal gas
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', applications: work, enthalpy and heat capacity

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Using the bond enthalpies H–H = 435 kJ mol⁻¹, Cl–Cl = 243 kJ mol⁻¹ and H–Cl = 431 kJ mol⁻¹, the enthalpy change for the reaction H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g) is:

solution.concept: ΔrH from bond enthalpies (gas-phase reaction)
solution.explanation: ΔrH = Σ(bond enthalpies of bonds broken) − Σ(bond enthalpies of bonds formed).
solution.why_others_wrong: +184 kJ subtracts in the wrong order. +247 kJ counts only one H–Cl bond formed. −92 kJ is the value per mole of HCl, not for the reaction as written.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', bond enthalpy

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (concentration term) with List-II (definition).

List-I:
A. Molarity
B. Molality
C. Mole fraction
D. Parts per million

List-II:
I. Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
II. Moles of solute per litre of solution
III. Parts of a component per 10⁶ parts of the solution
IV. Moles of a component divided by the total moles of all components

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Ways of expressing concentration
solution.explanation: Molarity uses the volume of the solution; molality uses the mass of the solvent; mole fraction is a ratio of moles; ppm is used for very small amounts.
steps: Molarity → mol per litre of solution → II
Molality → mol per kg of solvent → I
Mole fraction → moles of component / total moles → IV
ppm → parts per million parts → III
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', expressing concentration of solutions
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following liquid pairs forms a solution showing negative deviation from Raoult's law?

solution.concept: Non-ideal solutions: negative deviation
solution.explanation: Negative deviation occurs when the A–B attractions are stronger than A–A and B–B attractions. Chloroform forms a hydrogen bond with the oxygen of acetone, so the vapour pressure falls below the Raoult's law value.
steps: Chloroform + acetone: new H-bonds between unlike molecules → negative deviation
Ethanol + acetone: acetone breaks some H-bonds of ethanol → positive deviation
CS₂ + acetone: weaker unlike interactions → positive deviation
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', ideal and non-ideal solutions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The elevation of boiling point of a dilute solution depends on the chemical nature of the solute.
Statement II: Osmotic pressure measurement is preferred for finding the molar masses of proteins and other biomolecules.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Colligative properties and their uses
solution.explanation: Colligative properties depend only on the number of solute particles, not on their nature: Statement I is false. Osmotic pressure is measured at room temperature and is large even for very dilute solutions, so it suits biomolecules that are unstable at high temperatures and have large molar masses: Statement II is true.
steps: Boiling point elevation ΔTb = Kb m → depends on number of particles only → Statement I false
Osmotic pressure method used for proteins and polymers → Statement II true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', colligative properties and osmotic pressure
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 3.0 g of urea (molar mass 60 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved in 500 g of water. The freezing point of the solution is (K_f of water = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹; freezing point of water = 0 °C):

solution.concept: Depression of freezing point: ΔT_f = K_f × m
solution.explanation: Urea is a non-electrolyte (i = 1). Molality uses the mass of solvent in kilograms.
solution.why_others_wrong: −0.093 °C divides by 1 kg instead of 0.5 kg. −0.372 °C treats urea as if it gave two particles. −1.86 °C takes the molality as 1.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', depression of freezing point

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Two liquids A and B form an ideal solution. At a certain temperature the vapour pressures of pure A and pure B are 450 mm Hg and 700 mm Hg. For a solution in which the mole fraction of A is 0.4, the mole fraction of A in the vapour in equilibrium with it is:

solution.concept: Raoult's law and Dalton's law of partial pressures
solution.explanation: Each partial pressure is p° × x (Raoult). The vapour composition is the partial pressure divided by the total pressure (Dalton).
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.40 is the mole fraction in the liquid. 0.70 is y_B. 0.60 is x_B. The vapour is richer in the more volatile component B.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', vapour pressure of liquid–liquid solutions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The depression of freezing point of a 0.01 m aqueous KCl solution is nearly twice that of a 0.01 m aqueous glucose solution.
Reason (R): In dilute aqueous solution, KCl dissociates almost completely into K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, so its van't Hoff factor is close to 2.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: van't Hoff factor for electrolytes
solution.explanation: Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles. Each KCl unit gives two ions, while glucose stays as one molecule, so ΔT_f = i K_f m is nearly doubled for KCl. R is true and explains A.
steps: ΔT_f ∝ i → KCl shows nearly twice the depression
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', abnormal molar masses and van't Hoff factor
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following are true for an ideal solution of two liquids?

(a) The enthalpy of mixing is zero.
(b) The volume of mixing is zero.
(c) It obeys Raoult's law over the entire range of concentration.
(d) The A–B interactions are stronger than the A–A and B–B interactions.
(e) It forms a minimum-boiling azeotrope.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Ideal solutions
solution.explanation: In an ideal solution the A–B interactions are nearly equal to the A–A and B–B interactions, so no heat is absorbed or released and there is no volume change on mixing. Such solutions follow Raoult's law at all compositions. Azeotropes form only with large deviations from Raoult's law.
steps: (c) True: obeys Raoult's law at all compositions
(e) False: minimum-boiling azeotropes come from large positive deviation
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', ideal and non-ideal solutions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A salt of type AB₂ is 80% dissociated into A²⁺ and B⁻ ions in a 0.1 m aqueous solution. The depression of freezing point of this solution is (K_f of water = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹):

solution.concept: van't Hoff factor from degree of dissociation: i = 1 + α(n − 1)
solution.explanation: AB₂ → A²⁺ + 2B⁻ gives n = 3 particles per formula unit. Partial dissociation gives i between 1 and 3.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.186 K ignores dissociation (i = 1). 0.558 K assumes complete dissociation (i = 3). 0.335 K uses n − 1 = 1 as if the salt gave only two ions (i = 1.8).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', abnormal molar masses and van't Hoff factor

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A solution of 2.0 g of a protein in 250 mL of water has an osmotic pressure of 0.0246 atm at 300 K. The molar mass of the protein is (R = 0.082 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹):

solution.concept: Molar mass from osmotic pressure: π = (w/M)RT/V
solution.explanation: Rearrange to M = wRT/(πV), with V in litres to match R in L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 × 10³ ignores the volume (takes V = 1 L). 5.0 × 10² multiplies by V instead of dividing. 8.0 uses V = 250 without converting mL to L.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', osmosis and osmotic pressure

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a solute that associates in solution, the van't Hoff factor i is less than 1.
Statement II: Ethanoic acid dimerises in benzene through hydrogen bonding, so the molar mass found from colligative properties is about twice its true value.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Association and abnormal molar mass
solution.explanation: Association reduces the number of particles, so i = (normal molar mass)/(observed molar mass) is less than 1: Statement I is true. Two ethanoic acid molecules join by hydrogen bonds in benzene, halving the number of particles; the colligative effect halves and the calculated molar mass doubles (about 120 instead of 60): Statement II is true.
steps: Association → fewer particles → i < 1 → Statement I true
2CH₃COOH ⇌ (CH₃COOH)₂ in benzene → observed molar mass ≈ 2 × 60 → Statement II true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', abnormal molar masses
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The pH of a 0.005 M aqueous solution of Ba(OH)₂ at 298 K, assuming complete dissociation, is (K_w = 10⁻¹⁴; log 5 = 0.70):

solution.concept: pH of a strong base that gives two OH⁻ ions per formula unit
solution.explanation: Ba(OH)₂ → Ba²⁺ + 2OH⁻, so [OH⁻] is twice the concentration of the base.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 is the pOH, not the pH. 11.7 forgets that each Ba(OH)₂ gives two OH⁻ ions (pOH = 2.3). 2.3 is the pOH from that same mistake.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', the pH scale

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For the equilibrium N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH < 0, the yield of ammonia at equilibrium is increased by:

solution.concept: Le Chatelier's principle
solution.explanation: The forward reaction reduces the number of gas moles (4 → 2) and releases heat. Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles, so it shifts the equilibrium towards NH₃.
steps: Exothermic → higher temperature favours the reverse reaction
A catalyst speeds up both directions equally and does not change the equilibrium yield
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', factors affecting equilibria

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The Henry's law constants (K_H) of four gases W, X, Y and Z in water at the same temperature are 1.6, 35, 70 and 145 kbar respectively. At the same partial pressure, which gas is the most soluble in water?

solution.concept: Henry's law: p = K_H x
solution.explanation: At a fixed partial pressure p, the mole fraction of dissolved gas is x = p/K_H. The smaller K_H, the larger the solubility.
steps: Smallest K_H (1.6 kbar) → largest x → W is the most soluble
solution.why_others_wrong: Z has the largest K_H and is the least soluble; reading K_H as a solubility gets the order backwards.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', equilibrium involving dissolution of gases in liquids

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: BF₃ is a Lewis acid because it can accept a pair of electrons.
Statement II: The conjugate base of a strong acid is a strong base.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Lewis acids; conjugate acid–base pairs
solution.explanation: Boron in BF₃ has only six valence electrons and accepts an electron pair (for example from NH₃): Statement I is true. A strong acid gives up its proton easily, so its conjugate base has little tendency to take a proton back: it is a weak base. Statement II is false.
steps: BF₃: electron-deficient, accepts a lone pair → Lewis acid → Statement I true
Strong acid ↔ weak conjugate base (e.g. HCl / Cl⁻) → Statement II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', acids, bases and salts
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For which of the following equilibria is K_p equal to K_c?

solution.concept: Relation between K_p and K_c: K_p = K_c (RT)^Δn
solution.explanation: K_p = K_c when Δn, the change in the number of moles of gas, is zero.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', relationship between K_p and K_c

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 1.0 mol of H₂ and 1.0 mol of I₂ are heated in a closed 1.0 L vessel. At equilibrium, 1.5 mol of HI is present: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). The value of K_c is:

solution.concept: Equilibrium constant from an ICE table
solution.explanation: 2 mol of HI form from 1 mol each of H₂ and I₂, so forming 1.5 mol HI uses 0.75 mol of each.
steps: H₂ and I₂ used = 1.5/2 = 0.75 mol each
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 forgets to square [HI]. 9 leaves one of the reactant concentrations out of the denominator. 1/36 is K_c for the reverse reaction.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', equilibrium constant

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The pH of a 0.1 M solution of a weak monobasic acid HA (K_a = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵) is:

solution.concept: Ionisation of a weak acid: [H⁺] = √(K_a C) when α is small
solution.explanation: HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻. For a small degree of ionisation, K_a ≈ [H⁺]²/C.
steps: Check: α = 10⁻³/0.1 = 1%, small, so the approximation holds
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 is the pK_a. 6 forgets the square root (uses K_a C). 1 treats HA as a strong acid.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', ionisation of weak acids

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A buffer solution contains 0.2 M CH₃COOH and 0.1 M CH₃COONa. Its pH is (pK_a of CH₃COOH = 4.74; log 2 = 0.30):

solution.concept: Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for an acidic buffer: pH = pK_a + log([salt]/[acid])
solution.explanation: The acid is in excess over the salt, so the pH is below the pK_a.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.04 puts [acid]/[salt] in the log. 4.74 assumes equal concentrations. 9.26 is 14 − pK_a, as if it were a basic buffer.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', buffer solutions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (sparingly soluble salt) with List-II (K_sp in terms of its molar solubility s).

List-I:
A. AgCl
B. CaF₂
C. Al(OH)₃
D. Ca₃(PO₄)₂

List-II:
I. 27s⁴
II. 108s⁵
III. s²
IV. 4s³

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Solubility product: for MₓAᵧ, K_sp = xˣ yʸ s⁽ˣ⁺ʸ⁾
solution.explanation: Write the dissolution equation, express each ion concentration in terms of s, and multiply with powers equal to the coefficients.
steps: AgCl → Ag⁺ + Cl⁻: K_sp = s·s = s² → III
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', solubility equilibria of sparingly soluble salts
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Adding an inert gas at constant volume does not shift the equilibrium N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g).
Reason (R): Adding an inert gas at constant volume increases the total pressure of the system.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Effect of an inert gas on equilibrium
solution.explanation: At constant volume, the inert gas does not change the partial pressures (or molar concentrations) of N₂, H₂ and NH₃, so Q stays equal to K and nothing shifts: A is true. The total pressure does rise because more gas is present, so R is true. But the rise in total pressure is not why there is no shift; the reason is that the partial pressures of the reacting gases are unchanged.
steps: Constant V: partial pressures of N₂, H₂, NH₃ unchanged → no shift → A true
R does not explain A (if anything it would suggest a shift)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', effect of inert gas addition
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (salt dissolved in water) with List-II (nature of the solution at 298 K).

List-I:
A. NaCl
B. NH₄Cl
C. CH₃COONa
D. CH₃COONH₄

List-II:
I. Acidic (pH < 7)
II. Basic (pH > 7)
III. Neutral; salt of a strong acid and a strong base
IV. pH = 7 + ½(pK_a − pK_b)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Hydrolysis of salts
solution.explanation: Only ions from weak acids or weak bases hydrolyse. The cation of a weak base makes the solution acidic; the anion of a weak acid makes it basic; when both hydrolyse, the pH depends on pK_a and pK_b.
steps: CH₃COONH₄: both ions hydrolyse → pH = 7 + ½(pK_a − pK_b) → IV
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', hydrolysis of salts and the pH of their solutions
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Water can act both as a Brønsted acid and as a Brønsted base.
(b) The conjugate base of H₂SO₄ is SO₄²⁻.
(c) The ionic product of water, K_w, increases with rise in temperature.
(d) AlCl₃ is a Lewis base.
(e) The pH of pure water at 298 K is 7.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Acid–base concepts and the ionisation of water
solution.explanation: Water donates a proton to NH₃ and accepts one from HCl. The conjugate base of an acid is the acid minus one proton. Ionisation of water is endothermic, so K_w rises with temperature. AlCl₃ is electron-deficient and accepts electron pairs.
steps: (c) True: endothermic ionisation → K_w increases with T
(d) False: AlCl₃ is a Lewis acid
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', ionisation of acids and bases

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: N₂O₄(g) is 50% dissociated into NO₂(g) at equilibrium at a total pressure of 1.0 atm: N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g). K_p for this equilibrium at the same temperature is:

solution.concept: K_p from degree of dissociation using mole fractions
solution.explanation: Start with 1 mol N₂O₄. With α = 0.5, the total moles become 1 + α. Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure.
steps: At equilibrium: N₂O₄ = 1 − α = 0.5 mol, NO₂ = 2α = 1.0 mol, total = 1.5 mol
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 atm forgets that the total number of moles rises to 1 + α. 0.33 atm drops the factor 4 that comes from (2α)². 1.0 atm uses 4α²P without the (1 − α²) denominator.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', equilibrium constant in gaseous systems

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The solubility product of AgCl at 298 K is 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰. Its molar solubility in 0.01 M NaCl solution is (√1.8 = 1.34):

solution.concept: Common ion effect on solubility
solution.explanation: Cl⁻ from NaCl suppresses the dissolution of AgCl. Since s is tiny, [Cl⁻] ≈ 0.01 M.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.34 × 10⁻⁵ M is the solubility in pure water, ignoring the common ion. 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ M takes s = K_sp. 1.8 × 10⁻¹² M multiplies by 0.01 instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', common ion effect in the ionisation of salts

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 50 mL of 0.2 M HCl is mixed with 50 mL of 0.1 M NaOH at 298 K. The pH of the resulting solution is (log 2 = 0.30):

solution.concept: pH after partial neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong base
solution.explanation: H⁺ and OH⁻ neutralise mole for mole. The excess H⁺ is spread over the total volume of the mixture.
steps: Excess H⁺ = 5 mmol in 100 mL → [H⁺] = 0.05 M
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.00 forgets that the volume doubles (uses 50 mL). 0.70 ignores the neutralisation and uses 0.2 M. 12.70 treats the base as the reagent in excess.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: At a fixed temperature, the value of K_c for a reaction changes when the concentration of one of the reactants is increased.
Statement II: A catalyst increases the equilibrium constant of a reaction.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: What can and cannot change an equilibrium constant
solution.explanation: Adding a reactant changes Q, and the system shifts until Q = K again, but K itself depends only on temperature: Statement I is false. A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions equally; equilibrium is reached faster, but K is unchanged: Statement II is false.
steps: K_c depends only on temperature (for a given reaction as written) → Statement I false
Catalyst speeds up both directions equally → K unchanged → Statement II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', factors affecting equilibria
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about buffer solutions are correct? (pK_a of CH₃COOH = 4.74, pK_b of NH₄OH = 4.75)

(a) A mixture of CH₃COOH and CH₃COONa is an acidic buffer.
(b) A mixture of HCl and NaCl acts as a buffer.
(c) For an acidic buffer, pH = pK_a when the concentrations of the salt and the acid are equal.
(d) A buffer of pH about 9 can be prepared from CH₃COOH and CH₃COONa.
(e) A mixture of NH₄OH and NH₄Cl is a basic buffer.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Composition and pH range of buffers
solution.explanation: A buffer needs a weak acid with its salt (acidic buffer) or a weak base with its salt (basic buffer). By the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH = pK_a + log([salt]/[acid]); a weak acid–salt buffer works only within about one unit of its pK_a.
steps: (b) False: HCl is a strong acid; no reservoir to absorb added H⁺ or OH⁻
(d) False: an acetate buffer gives pH near 4.74 (about 3.7 to 5.7); pH 9 needs a basic buffer such as NH₄OH/NH₄Cl (pH = 14 − pK_b ≈ 9.25)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', buffer solutions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (element in a species) with List-II (its oxidation number).

List-I:
A. Mn in KMnO₄
B. Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇
C. P in H₃PO₃
D. N in NH₄⁺

List-II:
I. +6
II. −3
III. +7
IV. +3

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Rules for assigning oxidation numbers
solution.explanation: Take K = +1, H = +1 and O = −2, and set the sum of oxidation numbers equal to the charge on the species.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Redox Reactions', oxidation number
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following was used to provide electrical power in the Apollo space programme, with the water it produced being added to the astronauts' drinking water?

solution.concept: Fuel cells
solution.explanation: A fuel cell converts the energy of combustion of a fuel such as hydrogen directly into electrical energy. In the H₂–O₂ fuel cell the overall reaction is 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), so its only product is water. Such cells powered the Apollo spacecraft, and the water vapour formed was condensed and added to the drinking water.
steps: Overall reaction of the H₂–O₂ fuel cell: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
Only product: water → usable as drinking water
Used in the Apollo space programme
solution.why_others_wrong: The dry cell and the lead storage battery store a fixed amount of reactants and give no water; the Daniell cell is a laboratory cell that gives Zn²⁺ and Cu, not water.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', fuel cells

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The conductivity (κ) of an electrolyte solution increases on dilution.
Statement II: The molar conductivity of an aqueous KCl solution decreases on dilution.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Variation of conductivity and molar conductivity with concentration
solution.explanation: Conductivity is the conductance of a unit volume of solution; on dilution there are fewer ions per unit volume, so κ decreases: Statement I is false. Molar conductivity is the conductance of all the ions from one mole of electrolyte; for a strong electrolyte such as KCl, interionic attractions weaken on dilution, so Λm increases: Statement II is false.
steps: κ decreases on dilution (fewer ions per cm³) → Statement I false
Λm of KCl increases on dilution → Statement II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', variation of conductivity and molar conductivity with concentration
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Given the standard reduction potentials Li⁺/Li = −3.05 V, Zn²⁺/Zn = −0.76 V, Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V and Ag⁺/Ag = +0.80 V, the strongest reducing agent among the four metals is:

solution.concept: Electrochemical series
solution.explanation: The more negative the standard reduction potential, the less the ion wants to be reduced and the more readily the metal is oxidised, so the stronger the metal is as a reducing agent.
steps: Li loses electrons most readily → strongest reducing agent
solution.why_others_wrong: Ag has the most positive E°, so Ag⁺ is the best oxidising agent and Ag the weakest reducing agent.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', electrochemical series

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The limiting molar conductivities (in S cm² mol⁻¹) of HCl, HCOONa and NaCl at 298 K are 426, 105 and 126 respectively. The limiting molar conductivity of HCOOH (in S cm² mol⁻¹) is:

solution.concept: Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions
solution.explanation: Λ°m of an electrolyte is the sum of the limiting ionic conductivities of its ions. Combine the given values so that only H⁺ and HCOO⁻ remain.
solution.why_others_wrong: 657 adds all three. 447 adds NaCl and subtracts HCOONa, which leaves Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in the sum. 195 subtracts both salts from HCl.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', Kohlrausch's law and its applications

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For the cell Cu(s) | Cu²⁺(aq, 1 M) || Ag⁺(aq, 1 M) | Ag(s), the standard Gibbs energy change of the cell reaction is (E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V, E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹):

solution.concept: ΔG° = −nFE°cell
solution.explanation: Cell reaction: Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag, so two electrons are transferred. E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode.
solution.why_others_wrong: −44.4 kJ uses n = 1 (the 2 in 2Ag⁺ is not a reason to halve). +88.8 kJ has the wrong sign for a cell that works spontaneously. −220.0 kJ adds the two electrode potentials.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', cell potential and Gibbs energy of the reaction

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A conductivity cell with cell constant 1.29 cm⁻¹ shows a resistance of 100 Ω when filled with 0.1 M KCl solution. The molar conductivity of the solution is:

solution.concept: κ = G*/R and Λm = κ × 1000/C (κ in S cm⁻¹, C in mol L⁻¹)
solution.explanation: First get the conductivity from the cell constant and resistance, then convert to molar conductivity. The factor 1000 converts litres to cm³.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.129 leaves out the factor 1000. 12.9 uses C = 1 M. 1.29 × 10⁶ multiplies the cell constant by R instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', measurement of the conductivity of ionic solutions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The molar conductivity of acetic acid increases steeply on dilution.
Reason (R): The limiting molar conductivity of a weak electrolyte cannot be obtained by extrapolating its Λm versus √c graph to zero concentration.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Weak electrolytes: molar conductivity and degree of dissociation
solution.explanation: Acetic acid is a weak electrolyte. On dilution its degree of dissociation rises sharply, so the number of ions from one mole rises and Λm increases steeply: A is true. Because Λm rises so steeply near zero concentration, its graph against √c cannot be extrapolated; Λ°m is found with Kohlrausch's law instead: R is true. But R is a consequence of the steep rise, not its cause; the cause is the increase in the degree of dissociation.
steps: Weak electrolyte: α increases sharply on dilution → Λm rises steeply → A true
Λ°m found from Kohlrausch's law, not by extrapolation → R true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', variation of molar conductivity with concentration
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (electrode of a commercial cell) with List-II (reaction taking place at it).

List-I:
A. Anode of the dry (Leclanché) cell
B. Cathode of the dry (Leclanché) cell
C. Anode of the lead storage battery during discharge
D. Cathode of the hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell

List-II:
I. Pb(s) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → PbSO₄(s) + 2e⁻
II. O₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻(aq)
III. Zn(s) → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻
IV. MnO₂ + NH₄⁺ + e⁻ → MnO(OH) + NH₃

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Electrode reactions in the dry cell, lead storage battery and fuel cell
solution.explanation: Oxidation (loss of electrons) takes place at the anode and reduction (gain of electrons) at the cathode. The two oxidation half-reactions belong to the two anodes: zinc in the dry cell and lead in the lead storage battery. Of the two reductions, the one involving MnO₂ and NH₄⁺ belongs to the dry cell and the reduction of O₂ to OH⁻ in alkaline electrolyte to the fuel cell.
steps: Dry cell anode: the zinc container is oxidised, Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → III
Dry cell cathode: MnO₂ is reduced, MnO₂ + NH₄⁺ + e⁻ → MnO(OH) + NH₃ → IV
Lead storage battery anode (discharge): Pb + SO₄²⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2e⁻ → I
H₂–O₂ fuel cell cathode: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻ → II
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping the two dry-cell electrodes puts an oxidation at the cathode, and matching zinc to the lead battery (or lead to the dry cell) mixes up which metal each anode is made of.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', batteries and fuel cells
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The oxidation number of oxygen in OF₂ is +2.
(b) The oxidation number of oxygen in H₂O₂ is −1.
(c) The oxidation number of oxygen in KO₂ is −½.
(d) The oxidation number of hydrogen in NaH is +1.
(e) The reaction 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ is a disproportionation reaction.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Exceptions in oxidation numbers; disproportionation
